q: 101. Rotary is ideally suited .............
options: when traffic is more than 4 streams join at the junction
when the pedestrian traffic is heavy
explain: Rotaries (roundabouts) work best when multiple roads (more than 4) meet at a single junction, as they eliminate complex signal phases and multiple crossing conflicts.

q: 102. An elliptical rotary island is provided when .............
options: most of the traffic is along its major axis
most of the traffic is along its minor axis
right turning traffic is more than 25%
traffic density is more than 3000 vehicles/h
explain: Elliptical shapes are used when the traffic flow is significantly higher in one direction (the major axis), providing more weaving length for those primary streams.

q: 103. Grade separation had the advantage of .............
options: number of points of conflicts is nil
explain: Grade separation (flyovers/underpasses) physically separates crossing traffic, thereby reducing the number of intersection conflict points to zero.

q: 104. A disadvantage of 'Diamond junction' is .............
options: no provision for easy right turn
explain: In a standard diamond interchange, right-turning vehicles must still cross oncoming traffic at the terminal intersections on the minor road.

q: 105. A three level round about is preferred to a clover left junction when .............
options: left turn traffic has a direct path
heavy traffic is to be handled
construction of an over bridge is very difficult
explain: Cloverleaf interchanges require vast amounts of land for loops. A three-level roundabout is a more compact solution for high-capacity grade separation.

q: 106. For the most effective traffic control, adopt .............
explain: Too many signs can lead to information overload and driver distraction. Effective control relies on a limited number of clear, essential signs.

q: 107. Regulatory signs are .............
options: red circular dies 60 cm dia. placed 2.8 m above G.L.
red triangle 45 cm side with a rectangular plate below
rectangular yellow plates 75 cm x 120 cm with black letters
rectangular in shape but no definite size
explain: Mandatory or Regulatory signs (except Stop and Give Way) are circular in shape with a red border, standardizing their appearance for quick recognition.

q: 108. Unguarded level crossing comes under .............
explain: Hazardous conditions like an unguarded railway crossing are categorized as Warning (Cautionary) signs, typically triangular in shape.

q: 109. An advantage of traffic signal is .............
explain: Traffic signals ensure the orderly flow of traffic by allocating right-of-way to different movements in a predictable, timed sequence.

q: 110. A disadvantage of Traffic Signals is .............
options: traffic along one or two directions is permitted while the remaining has to wait
waiting vehicles let off exhaust gases into the environment
explain: Idling vehicles at red lights contribute significantly to local air pollution through increased exhaust emissions while waiting.

q: 111. Yellow colour of a 'Coloured light traffic signal' indicates .............
explain: The amber (yellow) light provides 'clearance time' for vehicles already in or near the intersection to pass through safely before the cross-traffic starts.

q: 112. Centre line for an urban road of more than 4 lanes is .............
options: 3 m long broken line with a gap of 4.5 m in between lines
two thick parallel lines with a gap of 75 mm in between
explain: On multi-lane urban roads, a double solid white or yellow line is used to strictly prohibit crossing into opposing traffic lanes.

q: 113. Thick white and black lines of 2 m to 4 m long provided along the width of a highway indicates ...........
explain: These longitudinal stripes (often called Zebra crossings) mark the legal area for pedestrians to cross the roadway.

q: 114. The inventor of road making as a building science, was .............
explain: Pierre-Marie-Jérôme Trésaguet (1716–1796) is often credited with establishing the first scientific approach to road construction in France.

q: 115. The road foundation for modern highway construction, was developed by .............
explain: Thomas Telford and John Loudon McAdam both contributed essential modern principles: Telford emphasized heavy foundations, while McAdam focused on surface drainage and size-graded stone.

q: 116. In water bound macadam roads, binding material, is .............
explain: WBM roads use stone screenings and stone dust, which—when mixed with water—act as a binder to fill the voids between larger aggregates.

q: 117. The full width of land acquired before finalizing a highway, alignment is known .............
explain: The Right of Way (ROW) is the total width of land acquired for the road, including the pavement, shoulders, and future expansion areas.

q: 118. The width of the right-of-way is decided so as to accommodate .............
explain: The primary component of the ROW is the formation width (the width of the top of the embankment or bottom of the cutting).

q: 119. The width formation of a road means the width of .............
explain: Formation width is the finished top width of the embankment or the bottom width of a cutting, excluding side drains.

q: 120. The pavement width of a road depends upon .............
explain: Pavement width is mathematically determined by multiplying the standard width of a single lane by the total number of lanes required for the traffic volume.

q: 121. The traffic carrying capacity of a single lane, depends on .............
explain: Lane capacity is influenced by vehicle speed and size, as well as external interruptions like intersections and railway crossings.

q: 122. If L is the length of vehicles in metres, C is the clear distance between two consecutive vehicles (stopping sight distance), V is the speed of vehicles in km/hour, the maximum number N of vehicles/hour, is .............
explain: The formula for basic capacity is C = 1000 * V / S, where S is the space headway (L + clear gap). Substituting L+C for S gives 1000V/(L+C).

q: 123. The convexity provided to the carriageway between the crown and edge of the pavement, is known as .............
explain: Camber (or cross-slope) is the transverse convexity provided to ensure water drains off the road surface.

q: 124. If the difference in elevation of an edge of the pavement 9 m wide and its crown is 15 cm, the camber o the pavement, is .............
explain: Camber is Rise / (Half-width). Rise = 0.15m. Half-width = 9/2 = 4.5m. Slope = 0.15 / 4.5 = 1 / 30.

q: 125. In scanty rainfall regions, the camber provided will be .............
explain: Where rainfall is low, a flatter camber is sufficient for drainage and provides better safety and comfort for vehicles.

q: 126. On concrete roads, the camber generally provided, is .............
explain: Concrete roads are smooth and impervious, so they require the flattest camber (1.3% to 1.7%), typically 1 in 60 to 1 in 72.

q: 127. On earth roads, the camber should preferably be .............
explain: Earthen roads are highly porous and susceptible to erosion, requiring a steep camber (5% to 6%) to shed water rapidly.

q: 128. Excessive camber on pavements may cause .............
options: slip of the speedy vehicles towards the edges
explain: Too much camber concentrates traffic in the center (causing wear), increases the risk of side-slipping, and speeds up runoff which erodes road shoulders (berms).

q: 129. Camber in pavements is provided by .............
options: straight at the edges and parabolic at the crown
explain: Depending on the pavement type, camber can be straight (for concrete), parabolic (for fast traffic), or a composite of both.

q: 130. On a pavement with parabolic camber, the angle of inclination of the vehicles will be .............
options: same at the edges as well as at the crown
explain: In a parabolic shape, the slope increases as you move from the center (crown) toward the edges, meaning vehicles at the edge are tilted more.

q: 131. The camber on pavements, is provided by .............
options: straight line and parabolic at crown
explain: The parabolic method is widely preferred for fast-moving traffic because it is very flat near the crown, making lane changes easier.

q: 132. If the elevations along a road increase, the slope of the road along the longitudinal direction, is known as .............
explain: An upward slope in the direction of travel is defined as a positive grade (upgrade), while a downward slope is a negative grade.

q: 133. The best compromise between the increase of the length of a highway and reduction in its load carrying capacity, is the ruling gradient .............
explain: 1 in 20 (5%) is often considered the ideal balance in hilly terrain, providing a decent gradient without significantly penalizing vehicle load capacity.

q: 134. Reduction of load capacity in a ruling gradient of .............
explain: A 1 in 20 gradient is estimated to reduce the effective load-carrying capacity of a standard commercial vehicle by approximately 10% compared to a flat road.

q: 135. The steepest gradient permitted on roads which, in ordinary conditions, does not exceed, is known .............
explain: The maximum (limiting) gradient is the steepest slope used when the ruling gradient is not feasible due to terrain or cost.

q: 136. Any gradient on a road is said to be an exceptional gradient, if it is .............
options: less than minimum gradient or more than maximum gradient
explain: Exceptional gradients exceed both ruling and limiting gradients; they are used only for very short stretches in extreme terrain.

q: 137. floating gradients are generally provided .............
explain: A floating gradient allows a vehicle to maintain its speed using its momentum without additional power, typically designed into summit curves.

q: 138. If A is the projected area of a vehicle in square metres, V is speed of the vehicles in kilometers per hour and C is a constant, then the wind resistance R to the moving vehicles, is given by ...........
explain: Aerodynamic (wind) resistance is proportional to the square of the velocity ($V^2$) and the frontal area of the vehicle.

q: 139. For a properly designed vehicle, the resistance generally ignored, is .............
explain: At standard highway speeds for commercial vehicles, wind resistance is often considered negligible compared to rolling and grade resistances in basic design calculations.

q: 140. If W is the weight of a vehicle negotiating an upgrade 1 : S along a track having co-efficient of resistance μ, the tractive force T is given by .............
explain: Based on the equilibrium of forces ($P = W 	imes (\mu + i)$), the tractive force required is the sum of rolling resistance and grade resistance.

q: 141. For calculating the tractive force along an upgrade of an asphalt road, the most probable value of the co-efficient of traction resistance μ is assumed .............
explain: For smooth asphalt roads, the rolling resistance coefficient ($\mu$) is typically taken as 1/30 (approx 0.033).

q: 142. Raising of outer edge of a road with respect to inner edges, is known .............
explain: Super-elevation, cant, and banking are all synonymous terms for the tilting of the roadway on a curve to counter centrifugal force.

q: 143. Raising of outer edge of a road with respect to inner edge, is known .............
explain: This is a repetition of Q.142; all terms refer to the transverse slope on a horizontal curve.

q: 144. If no super elevation is provided on a road along curves, pot holes may develop at .............
explain: Centrifugal force pushes the vehicle outward, increasing the pressure and wear on the outer edge of the pavement, leading to premature failure.

q: 145. The advantage of providing super-elevation on roads, is .............
options: reduced maintenance cost of the roads
explain: Super-elevation allows for higher safe speeds, which increases lane capacity (volume) and reduces lateral wear/tear on the pavement (maintenance).

q: 146. For a comfortable travel on Highways, the centrifugal ratio should not exceed .............
explain: The centrifugal ratio ($P/W$) is kept at a maximum of 0.25 for highways to ensure stability against overturning and comfort for passengers.

q: 147. The most commonly adopted method to provide super elevation on roads, is by pivoting the road surface about .............
options: outer edge so that the inner edge is lowered
crown so that outer edge is raised and inner edge is lowered
inner edge so that outer edge is raised
explain: Revolving the pavement about the inner edge is preferred because it doesn't change the drainage profile of the inner side and is easier to construct.

q: 148. Before providing super-elevation on roads, the portion of the carriageway between the crown and the outer edge is made .............
options: to have slope of the camber on the other half of the carriageway
explain: The first step in super-elevation transition is eliminating the outer camber by raising the outer edge until the outer half of the road is horizontal.

q: 149. The super-elevation on roads is .............
options: directly proportional to width of pavement
directly proportional to velocity of vehicles
inversely proportional to acceleration due to gravity
inversely proportional to the radius of curvature
explain: From the formula $e = V^2 / 127R$, it is mathematically clear that super-elevation ($e$) is inversely proportional to the radius ($R$).

q: 150. The maximum safe speed on roads, depends on the .............
explain: Safe speed is a function of the road classification (highway vs urban), the friction of the surface, and the geometric design of the curves.

q: 151. Non-passing sight distance along a road is the longest distance at which the driver of a moving vehicle, may see an obstacle on the pavement
explain: According to IRC standards, for calculating Stopping Sight Distance (Non-passing sight distance), the height of the object is taken as 0.15m (15cm) in some codes, but in this specific technical context/book, 25 cm is the standard provided value for the obstacle height.

q: 152. The ability of a driver to stop the vehicle moving with the designed speed, depends upon
explain: Stopping ability is a function of the PIEV theory (Perception, Intellection, Emotion, Volition) and the mechanical condition of the vehicle's braking system.

q: 153. For a vehicle moving with a speed of 80 km per hour, the brake reaction time, in ordinary cases, is
explain: The Indian Roads Congress (IRC) recommends a standard total reaction time of 2.5 seconds for the design of stopping sight distance.

q: 154. The efficiency of the brakes of a vehicle depends upon
explain: Braking efficiency is influenced by the friction between the tire and the road, which is affected by surface texture, tire tread, and the presence of moisture or lubricants.

q: 155. The distance travelled by a moving vehicle during perception and brake reaction times, is known as
explain: Lag distance is the distance covered during the total reaction time (t), calculated as v * t.

q: 156. Minimum stopping distance for moving vehicles on road with a design speed of 80 km/hour, is
explain: Using the SSD formula $v t + v^2 / (2gf)$, for a speed of 80 km/h and standard friction, the value approximates to 120 meters.

q: 157. If V is the velocity in km ph, t the brake reaction time in seconds and η the efficiency of the brakes, the stopping distance S of the vehicle, is
explain: This is a derivation of the SSD formula where 0.28V represents the conversion of km/h to m/s for the lag distance, and the second term accounts for braking distance adjusted for efficiency.

q: 158. Horizontal curves on highways are provided
options: to break the monotony of driving
to discourage the tendency to increase speed
to decrease the mental strain on drivers
explain: Curves are not just for terrain changes; they serve psychological purposes like preventing highway hypnosis and controlling speed.

q: 159. Design of horizontal curves on highways, is based on
options: permissible friction on the road surface
explain: The design must balance centrifugal force against available friction and super-elevation based on the design speed.

q: 160. The type of curves generally provided on highways, is
explain: Highway alignment consists of horizontal curves (often with transition curves) and vertical curves (summit and valley).

q: 161. The ideal shape of a transition curve, is
explain: The Clothoid (Spiral) is ideal because its radius decreases at the same rate as the length increases, providing a linear change in centrifugal acceleration.

q: 162. The shape of a vertical curve, is
explain: A square parabola is preferred for vertical curves because it provides a constant rate of change of grade.

q: 163. When an up gradient of a highway meets a downgrade, the vertical curve provided, is known as
explain: A summit curve (convex upwards) is formed when an ascending gradient meets a descending gradient.

q: 164. Degree of a road curve is defined as the angle in degrees subtended at the centre by an arc of
explain: In road works (IRC), the degree of curve is traditionally defined based on a 30-meter arc or chord length.

q: 165. If degree of a road curve is defined by assuming the standard length of an arc as 30 metres, the radius of 1° curve is equal
explain: The formula is $R = (30 \times 180) / (\pi 	imes D)$. For $D=1$, $R \approx 1718.87$ m, rounded to 1719 m.

q: 166. If the radii of a compound curve and a reverse curve are respectively the same, the length of common tangent
options: of compound curve will be more
of reverse curve will be more
of both curves will be equal
explain: Because the reverse curve turns in opposite directions, the geometry requires a longer common tangent to facilitate the change in direction compared to a compound curve.

q: 167. Widening of the roads on curves in hilly region, is done
options: on the outer and inner sides equally
less on outer side and more on inner side
explain: In hilly terrain, extra widening is usually provided entirely on the inner side of the curve due to topographical constraints.

q: 168. Full amount of extra width of a pavement on the curve, is provided at
explain: Widening is introduced gradually along the transition curve and reaches its full value at the start of the circular curve.

q: 169. If D is the degree of a curve, the percentage reduction of gradient, is
explain: Grade compensation is usually calculated as $(30+R)/R$ or $75/R$. In terms of degree $D$, it is often simplified in textbooks to 0.04 D.

q: 170. The radius of curvature provided along a transition curve, is
options: equal to the radius of circular curve
varying from infinity to the radius of circular curve
explain: A transition curve begins with a radius of infinity (straight line) and gradually decreases to the radius of the circular curve it meets.

q: 171. If the ruling gradient on any highway is 3%, the gradient provided on the curve of 300 metre radius, is
explain: Grade compensation = $75/300 = 0.25\%$. Compensated gradient = $3\% - 0.25\% = 2.75\%$.

q: 172. The length of a transition curve, is governed by
options: rate of change of radial acceleration
explain: Design takes the higher value from the comfort criteria (radial acceleration) and the appearance/safety criteria (super-elevation rate).

q: 173. The difference in gradients after full super-elevation and the initial alignment of a road, is known as
explain: In the context of the provided answer key, this refers to the 'differential gradient' created during the rotation of the pavement.

q: 174. An ideal vertical curve is
explain: While summit curves are parabolic, the cubic parabola is often cited in older texts as ideal for certain vertical transitions.

q: 175. In an ideal transition curve, the radius of curvature
options: is directly proportional to its distance from the point of commencement
is inversely proportional to the radius of main curve
is inversely proportional to the radius of main curve
explain: The fundamental property of a transition spiral is that the radius (r) is inversely proportional to the length (l) from the start ($rl = 	ext{constant}$).

q: 176. The standard equation of a cubic parabolic transition curve provided on roads, is
explain: The offset $y$ for a cubic parabola is given by $y = x^3 / (6RL)$.

q: 177. The standard equation of a cubic parabolic transition curve provided on roads, is
explain: Repeated question; the answer remains the cubic offset formula $x^3 / 6RL$.

q: 178. The ratio of maximum deviation angle and maximum polar deflection angle of a Lemniscate curve, is
explain: For a Lemniscate curve, the deviation angle ($\Delta$) is three times the polar deflection angle ($\alpha$).

q: 179. The maximum radial distance of a Lemniscate curve, having maximum polar angle α, is
explain: The polar equation of a Lemniscate is $r^2 = a^2 \cos 2	heta$, leading to the radial distance relation involving $\sin 2\alpha$.

q: 180. If a Lemniscate curve having an angle of deflection Δ, is transitional throughout, the maximum polar angle is
explain: As per the geometry of the Lemniscate used as a transition, the max polar angle is one-sixth of the deflection angle.

q: 181. In a right angle bend of a road provided with a transition throughout, the maximum polar angle will be
explain: For a $90^\circ$ bend, $\Delta = 90^\circ$. Max polar angle = $\Delta / 6 = 90 / 6 = 15^\circ$.

q: 182. If a Lemniscate curve of transition throughout is introduced to connect two parallel roads, the maximum polar angle of the curve, is
explain: Parallel roads involve a $180^\circ$ total turn. Applying the Lemniscate properties to this geometry results in a maximum polar angle of $30^\circ$.

q: 183. If R is the radius of a main curve and L is the length of the transition curve, the shift of the curve, is
explain: Shift (s) is calculated as $L^2 / 24R$.

q: 184. If L is the length of the transition curves provided on either side of a circular curve of radius R, the maximum angle of deflection with tangent for the junctions of the transition curve and circular curve, is
explain: The deflection angle at the end of the transition is $L / 2R$ radians, but the options provided usually require a specific conversion; 'none of these' is often chosen if the specific radiant/degree format isn't present.

q: 185. Setting out of Lemniscate transition curves, is done with
explain: Lemniscate curves are defined by polar coordinates, making polar deflection angles the natural choice for setting them out.

q: 186. The width of the right of way, is influenced by
explain: Right of way includes the entire land area acquired for the road, including the formation, shoulders, and future expansion space based on road class.

q: 187. The width of road pavements, depends upon
explain: Pavement width is a function of how many lanes are needed (traffic volume) and the width of each lane/median.

q: 188. Alignment of highways in hilly regions, is decided on
options: long stretch of very hard cutting
explain: Hill alignment is a balance of avoiding expensive cutting, bridge costs, and geological hazards.

q: 189. The first stage of deciding the alignment of a hill road, is
explain: Reconnaissance is always the initial stage to identify feasible routes.

q: 190. Reconnaissance is best done with the help of
explain: Aerial photography allows engineers to see terrain patterns and obstacles over large areas quickly.

q: 191. Selection of the routes, of highways depends upon
explain: All these factors influence the cost and functionality of the highway.

q: 192. During last phase of the reconnaissance, details of the grade line is recorded on 2 metre poles to indicate
options: distance between the previous and forward pegs
explain: The poles help visualize the vertical and horizontal path before moving to the 'trace-out' stage.

q: 193. Deviation of the alignment of a trace cut may be permitted in areas involving
explain: If the trace cut reveals an active landslide zone, the alignment must be deviated for safety.

q: 194. First operation during the detailed survey of a hill road, is
options: adjustment of alignment along with curves
explain: Setting up Bench Marks (BM) is the fundamental first step to ensure all subsequent leveling and surveys are tied to a known datum.

q: 195. The usual width of parapet walls along Highways in hilly region, is
explain: 60 cm is the standard width for safety parapets along hill road edges.

q: 196. The usual width of side drains along Highways in hilly region, is
explain: Standard hill road drains are typically 60 cm wide (often trapezoidal or V-shaped).

q: 197. The minimum value of camber provided for thin bituminous surface hill road, is
explain: For thin bituminous surfaces, the IRC recommended camber is $2.5\%$.

q: 198. Maximum super-elevation of hill roads should not exceed
explain: For hilly terrain (not snow-bound), the maximum super-elevation allowed is $10\%$.

q: 199. Super-elevation on roads in snow bound areas, should generally not exceed
explain: In snow-bound areas, super-elevation is restricted to $7\%$ to prevent slow-moving vehicles from sliding inward on ice.

q: 200. The type of transition curves generally provided on hill roads, is
explain: The spiral (clothoid) is the most commonly used transition curve on hill roads due to its superior comfort properties.
